S1 is a single-group formative study, appropriately classified as other: interviews, graph-based LLM prototype interaction, and follow-up feedback; no randomized assignment or scored creativity/diversity outcome is reported (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1-3.5).

S1 recruited five students aged 18?22, comprising 2 male and 3 female participants, all in writing-related fields with writing and LLM experience. The paper does not separately state an analyzed denominator or randomized count, supporting the null count fields (PDF p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 4, Section 3.3).

S1 participants modified and reorganized a familiar story through a graph-based LLM prototype; prototype interaction lasted 30 minutes, with interviews before and after it. The formative prototype model is not specified (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3.2).

S2 is a fixed-order within-person comparison, appropriately classified as quasi_people: ?Participants first wrote a story using ChatGPT and then completed the same task using our system.? Thus has_randomized_people_study is false (PDF p. 7, Section 5.2).

S2 recruited 16 students aged 18 to 22, comprising 8 male and 8 female participants; the response bars support 16 analyzed in each condition, representing the same 16 people, not separate groups or counts of stories. Randomized counts correctly remain null, and fewer than 50 people were analyzed (PDF p. 7, Sections 5.1-5.2; p. 8, Figure 5; p. 9, Figure 7).

The main participants studied writing-related fields, had advanced writing skills and familiarity with AI writing tools, and had not participated in a prior study involving this system. The methods and limitations support students despite the abstract describing professional and semi-professional writers (PDF p. 1, Abstract; p. 7, Section 5.1; p. 10, Section 7, Participant population).

Each S2 session lasted approximately one hour in a private room with researcher support; participants performed the same story-writing task from provided ideas using a think-out-loud protocol. Per-condition durations are not stated (PDF p. 7, Section 5.2).

GraphStory generates complete narrative text using GPT-4o and supports graph editing, AI-added event review, and multiple narrative flows; the ChatGPT baseline model is not specified (PDF p. 6, Sections 4.3-4.4; p. 7, Section 5.2).

The quantitative evaluation consists of participant questionnaires about tool interaction/functionality and NASA-TLX perceived workload, supplemented by interviews; none is a creativity or across-person diversity score on participants? stories. Figure 5 Q3 concerns efficiency in providing useful plot points; Figure 7 Q4 concerns alignment with chosen nodes (PDF p. 7, Sections 5.2-5.3.3; pp. 8-9, Figures 5-7; p. 9, Section 5.4).

S2-O1 and the one-line finding match Figure 5 Q3 exactly: GraphStory M = 6.25 (SD = 1.03), ChatGPT M = 5.62 (SD = 1.05); the text reports p < 0.05. These are participant tool-support ratings on a 7-point scale (PDF p. 8, Figure 5, Q3 and caption; p. 7, Section 5.3.1).
S2-O2 matches Figure 5 Q2 exactly: GraphStory M = 6.50 (SD = 0.71), ChatGPT M = 4.38 (SD = 1.41); the text reports p < 0.001 for ease of iteration (PDF p. 8, Figure 5, Q2; p. 7, Section 5.3.1).
S2-O3 matches Figure 5 Q4 exactly: GraphStory M = 6.44 (SD = 0.61), ChatGPT M = 5.25 (SD = 1.52); the text reports p < 0.01 for task efficiency (PDF p. 8, Figure 5, Q4; p. 7, Section 5.3.1).

The reported test is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and the comparative questionnaire uses a 7-point Likert scale, as stated in all three reported strings (PDF p. 7, Sections 5.3 and 5.3.1; p. 8, Figure 5).

Core eligibility = no and context_class = none are supported: neither study randomizes AI assistance or has at least 50 analyzed people, and outcomes are self-reports/qualitative feedback rather than scored creative output. This is an original system/user-study paper, not a synthesis, so the blank synthesis fields are appropriate (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3; pp. 7-9, Section 5; codebook Section 3).
